govdocs-archive_org-WARREN_COMMISSION_VO:
Volume XVIII of the Warren Commission hearings holds exhibits 885 through 1053 of the official inquiry into the assassination of President John F. Kennedy. The commission worked under Executive Order 11130, and the United States Government Printing Office printed its volumes.

Unlike the testimony volumes, this one is documentary: photographs, letters, reports, and records entered as evidence and numbered as exhibits. Researchers use these pages to check claims about the assassination against the papers the commission actually had in hand. It is a public record, complete as issued, and one of the most consulted parts of the Warren Report apparatus.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ComputersAboutT: A Giant Step for Mankind?: the publisher's insert - the made public government document on computers. Subject: government records. A single insert, kept complete. Dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of publishing ephemera and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDistrictofCo: An interview in the Daily Rag, an underground newspaper, carries the headline FBI Informer Confesses. Its subject is Robert Merritt, who spoke about his work as an FBI informer. The surviving record gives the paper, the headline, and the man's name. It gives no date or detail of what he confessed. The piece stands as an underground-press interview with a Bureau source.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HersheyRobertBo: FBI agents interviewed Robert Bowman Hershey on August 3, 1964, during the summer the Warren Commission finished its work. Interviews of named men fill the Bureau's assassination files by the thousand. The surviving record gives Hershey's name and the interview date but no subject or findings, so the entry stands as a dated FBI interview record from that investigation summer.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PawtaucketPubli:
Harold Weisberg wrote on September 24, 1975, to Carl Bohling of the Pawtucket Public Library in Rhode Island. He discusses Frank Sturgis, the Watergate burglar whose name crossed into assassination research. Weisberg mentions his own files dating to 1966-67. He also raises a matter he calls the 'Lucker Trust Fund.'

Letters to librarians were part of Weisberg's method. Libraries held his books, hosted his talks, and sometimes held his papers' future. This one carries case talk and archive talk together. The Sturgis reference dates from the years when Watergate and Dallas research were merging in the public mind, and a small library in Rhode Island was one stop on that circuit.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StLouisPost-Dis: James C. Millstone, assistant managing editor of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, wrote a letter dated August 18, 1972. The letter survives as a single piece of newspaper correspondence from a senior editor of a major Midwestern daily. It belongs to the paper trail of working journalists in the early 1970s, when letters like this one handled the business that phone calls left unrecorded.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WebsterRobertEd: An FBI memo dated February 7, 1964, summarizes the bureau's interviews with Robert Edward Webster, a man from Ohio. Webster had lived in the Soviet Union and returned, which drew official attention after Oswald's own defection story became famous. Agents compared such cases while testing Oswald's past. The memo gathers what Webster told them into one dated summary for the files.
govdocs-archive_org-sub-2-doc-0000017415: Invoice 11 for MKULTRA Subproject 2 went to the CIA's Chief of Finance Division in August 1957. MKULTRA was the agency's secret program of mind-control research, run for twenty years. Most of its files were destroyed in 1973, which makes each surviving paper matter. An invoice sounds dull, but it proves money moved for a named piece of the program. Such fragments are how the program's history gets rebuilt.
